A.explanation: A steadily increasing $F$ cannot be correct because the force must fall back to zero when the ball leaves the table.

B.explanation: A large $F$ at $t=0$ cannot be correct because contact has just started and deformation is still zero.

C.explanation: A smooth rise from zero to a maximum and back to zero matches increasing then decreasing deformation during the bounce.

D.explanation: A maximum $F$ at $t=0$ that only decreases cannot be correct because the ball must first be stopped and then re-accelerated upward.

hints: Notice $t=0$ is the instant the ball first touches the table, so ask what the contact force $F$ must be before any squashing occurs.
Connect squashing of the rubber ball to $F$: the ball is brought to rest and then pushed upward, so deformation and $F$ must build to a peak near mid-contact.
Check how the contact ends: the ball leaves the table, so $F$ must return to zero, giving a rise-and-fall shape rather than a line that starts high or keeps rising.
walkthrough: Identify the time interval: from first touch at $t=0$ to lift-off at the end of contact, so $F=0$ at both the start and the finish.
State the physics: the table force deforms the rubber ball, and larger deformation gives larger $F$, with impulse equal to the area under the $F$ against $t$ graph.
Follow the motion: on landing the downward speed is stopped as squashing increases, so $F$ rises from zero to a maximum at maximum squash.
Then the ball un-squashes and is accelerated upward, so $F$ decreases back to zero as contact is lost.
This requires a curve starting at the origin, rising smoothly to one peak and returning to zero, with no sudden jump. This is option C.
